title: Module 3 · IV Room and USP 797
intro: Your yearly sterile compounding competency (garbing, fingertip testing, media fill), rooms and air, cleaning, BUDs, vials, hazardous drugs, vincristine, diluent catches, parenteral nutrition and the final check.

cases.title: Your sterile compounding competency
cases.stem: Before you can compound alone in the IV room, you must pass the sterile compounding competency. You will repeat parts of it on a schedule as long as you work there.

steps.q: What does the competency include?

options.t: Training and a written or knowledge test
options.why: Initially, then at least every 12 months (USP 797).

options.t: Garbing and hand hygiene, with gloved fingertip and thumb sampling
options.why: Proves you can put on garb without contaminating your gloves.

options.t: Aseptic manipulation: a media fill test, then gloved fingertip sampling and a surface sample of your work area
options.why: Proves your technique keeps a product sterile.

options.t: A typing speed test
options.why: Not part of USP 797.

steps.q: Before compounding alone the first time, how many gloved fingertip tests must you pass after garbing, and what result passes?

options.t: Three separate times, each with zero colony forming units (CFU)
options.why: Initial garbing qualification: three consecutive passes, action level is any growth above 0 CFU.

options.t: One time, up to 5 CFU
options.why: The first qualification is stricter: three times, zero growth.

options.t: None if you passed in pharmacy school
options.why: Each site qualifies its own compounders.

steps.teach: Zero growth means your gloves stayed clean while you garbed. That is the point of the whole sequence.
steps.where: St. Mary's IV room competency SOP and the IV room supervisor or trainer.

steps.q: After the media fill test, the gloved fingertip action level is:

options.t: More than 3 CFU (total from both hands) fails
options.why: After a media fill, a small amount of growth is allowed. Above 3 CFU triggers retraining and retesting.

options.t: More than 0 CFU fails
options.why: That is the action level after garbing.

options.t: More than 20 CFU fails
options.why: Far too loose.

steps.q: How often must you repeat garbing and aseptic manipulation competency if you compound Category 1 and 2 CSPs?

options.t: At least every 6 months
options.why: Category 3 compounders repeat every 3 months. Training and knowledge assessment repeat at least every 12 months.

options.t: Every 2 years
options.why: Much more often than that.

options.t: Only once
options.why: Competency is ongoing.

cases.pearl: **Garb: 3 passes at 0 CFU to start. Media fill fingertip: above 3 CFU fails. Repeat every 6 months (Cat 1 and 2), training every 12 months.**

cases.title: Garbing in the right order
cases.stem: You walk into the ante room to garb.

steps.q: What is the principle behind the garbing order?

options.t: Dirtiest to cleanest: start with what is closest to the floor and the dirtiest parts of you
options.why: Shoe covers and hair covers go on before you wash, so you do not touch clean hands to dirty items.

options.t: Cleanest to dirtiest
options.why: Reversed.

steps.q: Put these in order: gown, shoe covers, wash hands, sterile gloves, hair cover and face mask.

options.t: Shoe covers, hair cover, face mask, wash hands, gown, sterile gloves
options.why: Gloves go on last, inside the buffer area or at the line of demarcation per SOP, and are sanitized with sterile 70% isopropyl alcohol.

options.t: Gloves, gown, wash hands, hair cover, shoe covers
options.why: Gloves first would contaminate them immediately.

options.t: Wash hands, gown, shoe covers, gloves, mask
options.why: You would touch your shoes after washing.

steps.teach: Your SOP is the final word on the exact order and where the line of demarcation is.
steps.where: St. Mary's garbing SOP (posted in the ante room).

steps.q: How long is the hand wash?

options.t: At least 30 seconds with soap and water, nails cleaned, hands to elbows
options.why: Then dry with low lint towels and apply an alcohol based hand rub before sterile gloves.

options.t: 5 seconds
options.why: Too short.

steps.q: What do you use on your gloves during compounding?

options.t: Sterile 70% isopropyl alcohol, applied often, especially after touching anything outside the hood
options.why: Let it dry. Wet alcohol is not yet working.

options.t: Nothing once gloves are on
options.why: Gloves pick up contamination; you sanitize them again and again.

cases.pearl: **Dirty to clean: shoes, hair, mask, wash 30 seconds, gown, sterile gloves, sterile IPA.**

cases.title: Media fill: what it proves
cases.stem: Your trainer hands you bags and vials of growth medium (soybean casein digest) instead of real drugs.

steps.q: What is the media fill test for?

options.t: To prove your aseptic technique by copying your most complex real manipulations with a growth medium
options.why: If any bacteria get in, the medium turns cloudy after incubation.

options.t: To test the hood airflow
options.why: That is certification of the hood.

steps.q: After incubation the medium is cloudy (turbid). What does that mean?

options.t: Failure: contamination got in. You stop compounding, get retrained, and repeat the full aseptic manipulation competency
options.why: If any part of the aseptic manipulation assessment fails, the whole assessment is repeated.

options.t: Normal; the medium is supposed to turn cloudy
options.why: Clear means pass. Cloudy means growth.

steps.q: How is a media fill usually incubated under the 2023 chapter?

options.t: At 20 to 25 °C and 30 to 35 °C, at least 7 days each (14 days total)
options.why: Two temperature ranges catch both environmental organisms and organisms from skin. Follow your SOP for the order.

options.t: One hour in the refrigerator
options.why: Bacteria will not grow there.

cases.pearl: **Media fill: copy your hardest work with growth medium. Clear = pass. Cloudy = fail and repeat everything.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)

cases.title: Rooms, ISO classes and pressure
cases.stem: On your tour you see the hood, the buffer room and the ante room.

steps.q: Match the area to its ISO class.

options.t: Hood (primary engineering control) ISO 5; buffer room ISO 7; ante room ISO 8 (ISO 7 if it opens into a negative pressure buffer room)
options.why: Lower ISO number = cleaner air.

options.t: All ISO 5
options.why: Only the hood is ISO 5.

options.t: Hood ISO 8, buffer ISO 5
options.why: Reversed.

steps.q: Which way should air flow between the buffer room and ante room for non hazardous compounding?

options.t: From the buffer room out to the ante room (buffer room positive pressure, at least 0.02 inch water column)
options.why: Positive pressure pushes dirty air away from where you compound.

options.t: From the ante room into the buffer room
options.why: That would pull dirtier air in.

steps.q: What is "first air"?

options.t: The HEPA filtered air coming out of the hood before it touches anything
options.why: Never block first air with your hands or other items between the filter and the critical site (needle, vial stopper, syringe tip).

options.t: The air in the ante room
options.why: No.

steps.teach: Most contamination in a working hood comes from the compounder blocking first air or touching critical sites.

cases.pearl: **ISO 5 hood, ISO 7 buffer, ISO 8 ante. Buffer positive. Never block first air.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)
Florida DOH: USP 797 inspection checklist (2024)

cases.title: Environmental monitoring and certification
cases.stem: The IV room supervisor shows you the monitoring binder.

steps.q: How often are the hoods and cleanroom certified?

options.t: At least every 6 months, and after major repairs or relocation
options.why: Certification checks airflow, HEPA filter integrity, particle counts and pressure.

options.t: Every 5 years
options.why: Much more often.

steps.q: Under the 2023 chapter, how often is surface sampling done in classified areas and hoods?

options.t: At least monthly
options.why: Viable air sampling is at least every 6 months.

options.t: Once a year
options.why: Too infrequent.

steps.q: A surface sample from the hood work surface grows mold. What happens?

options.t: It exceeds the action level: investigate, clean and disinfect (with a sporicidal agent), resample, and document corrective action
options.why: Any mold in an ISO 5 area needs investigation.

options.t: Ignore it if the count is low
options.why: Mold in ISO 5 is always a concern.

cases.pearl: **Certify every 6 months. Surface sample monthly. Air sample every 6 months.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)

cases.title: Cleaning the hood
cases.stem: It is the start of your IV room shift.

steps.q: What three steps make up cleaning under USP 797?

options.t: Cleaning (remove residue), disinfecting (kill microbes) and applying sterile 70% IPA to remove residue
options.why: Some products clean and disinfect in one step; follow the product's contact (dwell) time.

options.t: Just spray alcohol and wipe immediately
options.why: Alcohol alone does not clean residue, and wiping before the dwell time ends means it did not work.

steps.q: Which direction do you clean the hood?

options.t: From the cleanest area to the dirtiest: top to bottom, back to front, away from the HEPA filter
options.why: You move contamination out of the hood, not deeper in.

options.t: From the front edge to the back
options.why: That pushes dirt toward the critical work area.

steps.q: How often is a sporicidal agent used in the hood?

options.t: At least monthly (and when contamination is suspected)
options.why: Spores resist ordinary disinfectants.

options.t: Never
options.why: Required on a schedule.

cases.pearl: **Clean, disinfect, IPA. Top to bottom, back to front. Sporicidal monthly.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)

cases.title: Immediate use in an emergency
cases.stem: During a code, a nurse needs an amiodarone infusion mixed outside the IV room.

steps.q: What are the immediate use rules?

options.t: No more than 3 different sterile products, simple aseptic technique, and administration must start within 4 hours of starting preparation
options.why: USP 797 immediate use. Label with ingredients, preparer and the 4 hour limit unless given right away.

options.t: Any number of products, use within 24 hours
options.why: That is not immediate use.

steps.q: Why is the window so short?

options.t: The product was made outside clean air, so bacteria have little time to grow before it is used
options.why: Short time limits the risk.

options.t: Amiodarone loses potency in 4 hours
options.why: The limit is about sterility, not stability.

cases.pearl: **Immediate use: 3 products max, start within 4 hours.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)

cases.title: Category 1 or Category 2?
cases.stem: You prepare cefazolin 2 g in 100 mL NS in a hood located in a segregated compounding area (not a cleanroom suite).

steps.q: What category is this, and what is the maximum BUD?

options.t: Category 1: up to 12 hours at room temperature or 24 hours refrigerated
options.why: A hood in a segregated compounding area can only make Category 1.

options.t: Category 2: 10 days refrigerated
options.why: Category 2 needs a hood inside a classified cleanroom suite.

steps.q: The same bag made in the cleanroom suite from all sterile ingredients, no sterility test. Maximum BUD?

options.t: Category 2: 4 days room temperature, 10 days refrigerated, 45 days frozen
options.why: USP 797 (2023) Category 2, aseptically processed, sterile starting components, no sterility testing.

options.t: 90 days refrigerated
options.why: Far beyond the chapter limits.

steps.q: If any starting ingredient is nonsterile (for example a bulk powder), the Category 2 BUD drops to:

options.t: 1 day room temperature, 4 days refrigerated, 45 days frozen
options.why: Nonsterile starting components shorten the BUD.

options.t: No change
options.why: It is shorter.

steps.q: What also limits the BUD besides the USP category?

options.t: Chemical and physical stability of the drug in that diluent and container
options.why: The BUD is the shorter of the sterility limit and the stability limit. Check the label or Trissel's.

options.t: Nothing
options.why: Some drugs (for example ampicillin) are stable only hours.

cases.pearl: **Cat 1: 12 h room, 24 h fridge. Cat 2 sterile ingredients: 4 / 10 / 45 days. Always the shorter of sterility and stability.**

cases.title: Single dose and multiple dose vials
cases.stem: A single dose vial of ondansetron was punctured in the hood 6 hours ago. A multiple dose vial of insulin was opened 20 days ago.

steps.q: Can you use the single dose vial again?

options.t: Yes, if it was opened and kept in ISO 5 air, up to 12 hours after first puncture
options.why: If punctured outside ISO 5, it must be used within 1 hour.

options.t: No, single dose means use once only, no exceptions
options.why: USP 797 allows up to 12 hours inside ISO 5.

steps.q: Can the multiple dose vial still be used?

options.t: Yes: 28 days after opening unless the manufacturer states otherwise
options.why: Date the vial when opened.

options.t: No: 7 days maximum
options.why: The default is 28 days.

cases.pearl: **Single dose vial: 12 h inside ISO 5, 1 h outside. Multiple dose vial: 28 days.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 797, Pharmaceutical Compounding: Sterile Preparations (2023 revision)

cases.title: Hazardous drug compounding
cases.stem: An order arrives for cyclophosphamide, a NIOSH listed antineoplastic.

steps.q: Where is it compounded?

options.t: In a containment hood (biological safety cabinet or CACI) inside a negative pressure room
options.why: Negative pressure keeps hazardous drug out of the rest of the pharmacy.

options.t: In the regular positive pressure hood
options.why: Positive pressure would push hazardous drug toward people.

steps.q: What protective equipment do you wear?

options.t: Two pairs of chemotherapy gloves tested to ASTM D6978
options.why: Change gloves on a schedule and when torn.

options.t: A disposable gown shown to resist hazardous drug permeation, closing in the back
options.why: Not a cloth lab coat.

options.t: A closed system transfer device when the dosage form allows (required for administration, recommended for compounding)
options.why: Reduces aerosol and spill exposure.

options.t: One pair of exam gloves
options.why: Not protective enough.

steps.q: A nurse calls about a hazardous drug bag that leaked on the floor. What do you tell them?

options.t: Use the hazardous drug spill kit with full PPE, contain from the outside in, and dispose of waste as hazardous
options.why: Know where the spill kit is before you need it.

options.t: Wipe it with paper towels and throw them in the trash
options.why: Unsafe exposure and improper disposal.

cases.pearl: **Hazardous drugs: negative pressure, double chemo gloves, chemo gown, CSTD, spill kit.**

sources.t: USP General Chapter 800, Hazardous Drugs: Handling in Healthcare Settings
St. Mary's IV room SOPs, BUD policy and competency program (verify locally)

cases.title: Vincristine: the never event
cases.stem: A vincristine dose is ready to dispense. The oncology nurse asks for it in a syringe "to make it faster."

steps.q: How must vincristine be dispensed?

options.t: In a minibag (for example 25 to 50 mL), never a syringe
options.why: Given intrathecally by mistake, vincristine is almost always fatal. A minibag cannot be connected to a spinal needle.

options.t: In a syringe labeled "For IV use only"
options.why: Labels alone have failed; the minibag is the safeguard.

cases.call: Explain the reason calmly: "Vincristine is fatal if it is ever given into the spine, and the minibag makes that impossible. It is ready now in a minibag."

sources.t: ISMP: vincristine labeling and packaging changes to prevent wrong route (minibag dispensing)

cases.title: Diluent catches
cases.stem: Four orders are waiting for your final check.

steps.q: Which of these are diluent errors?

options.t: Phenytoin in D5W
options.why: Phenytoin precipitates in dextrose. Use normal saline only, with a 0.22 micron in line filter, no faster than 50 mg/min in adults.

options.t: Liposomal amphotericin B in normal saline
options.why: Saline breaks the liposomes. Use D5W only, and flush lines with D5W.

options.t: Ampicillin in D5W for a long infusion
options.why: Ampicillin is much less stable in dextrose; normal saline is preferred.

options.t: Vancomycin in normal saline
options.why: Vancomycin is fine in NS or D5W.

steps.q: Nitroglycerin infusion: which container?

options.t: Glass or non PVC (polyolefin) bag with non PVC tubing
options.why: Nitroglycerin is absorbed into PVC plastic, so the patient gets less drug.

options.t: Any standard PVC bag
options.why: Loses drug into the plastic.

cases.pearl: **Phenytoin NS only. Ampho B D5W only. Ampicillin NS. Nitro: no PVC.**

sources.t: St. Mary's IV room SOPs, BUD policy and competency program (verify locally)

cases.title: Parenteral nutrition: calcium and phosphate
cases.stem: You are checking an adult PN order with high calcium and phosphate.

steps.q: What is the main precipitation risk?

options.t: Calcium phosphate crystals, which can block lung vessels and have caused deaths
options.why: Check solubility with your compounder software or curves; temperature, pH, amino acid concentration and order of mixing all matter.

options.t: None
options.why: Calcium phosphate precipitation is a known fatal risk.

steps.q: Which filter for a 3 in 1 PN (lipids in the bag)?

options.t: 1.2 micron filter
options.why: Lipid droplets clog a 0.22 micron filter. 2 in 1 PN (no lipid) uses 0.22 micron.

options.t: 0.22 micron
options.why: Too small for lipid emulsions.

steps.q: What osmolarity limit applies for peripheral PN?

options.t: About 900 mOsm/L or less
options.why: Higher osmolarity damages peripheral veins; it needs a central line.

options.t: 2,000 mOsm/L
options.why: That needs a central line.

cases.pearl: **PN: watch Ca and Phos. 1.2 micron for lipids. Peripheral 900 mOsm/L max.**

sources.t: ASPEN parenteral nutrition safety consensus (Ayers P, et al. JPEN 2014;38:296-333)
St. Mary's IV room SOPs, BUD policy and competency program (verify locally)

cases.title: Final check of a CSP
cases.stem: A technician hands you a finished potassium chloride bag for your final check.

steps.q: What do you verify?

options.t: The right drug, concentration and volume match the order, using the vials, syringe pull back, images or gravimetric data per SOP
options.why: You verify what went in, not just the label.

options.t: Label: patient, drug, concentration, total volume, BUD, storage, and any high alert warning
options.why: The label is what the nurse trusts.

options.t: Visual inspection: no particles, cloudiness, leaks or color change
options.why: Hold the bag against light and dark backgrounds.

options.t: The technician's word that it is right
options.why: Your check is independent.

steps.q: The label says 40 mEq in 100 mL "for peripheral use." What is wrong?

options.t: Concentrated potassium (40 mEq/100 mL) is a central line concentration; peripheral rates are usually limited to 10 mEq/h
options.why: Call before it leaves the IV room.

options.t: Nothing
options.why: This mismatch can burn a vein or cause dangerous rates.

cases.pearl: **Final check: what went in, the label, and a look at the bag.**

cases.title: Shift simulation: IV room at 0600
cases.stem: At 0600: (1) a first dose cefepime for a septic patient; (2) the morning batch of 40 routine piggybacks; (3) your hood certification sticker expired yesterday; (4) a TPN due at 2100.

steps.q: What is the problem you must solve before compounding anything?

options.t: The hood certification lapsed; tell your supervisor and follow the SOP (use a certified hood, or limit to what policy allows)
options.why: Compounding in an uncertified hood violates USP 797.

options.t: Nothing; certification is paperwork
options.why: It proves the air is clean.

steps.q: Then what goes first?

options.t: The first dose cefepime for the septic patient
options.why: First doses for sepsis are time critical.

options.t: The TPN
options.why: Due at 2100.

options.t: The batch
options.why: Routine.

cases.pearl: **Clean air first, then first doses, then batch, then later items.**
